title: Practice: Greenhouse Gases and Climate Change

questions.stem: The greenhouse effect is a natural process that keeps Earth warm. Some students think all greenhouse effect is bad. Why is the natural greenhouse effect actually essential?

options.text: It prevents all radiation from reaching Earth's surface
Without it, Earth's average temperature would be about -18°C instead of +15°C, making it too cold for most life
It creates the ozone layer
It produces oxygen for us to breathe

questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect is vital — greenhouse gases in the atmosphere absorb infrared radiation re-emitted by Earth's surface and re-radiate it in all directions, including back towards Earth. Without this warming effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about -18°C. The problem is the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by human activities increasing greenhouse gas concentrations.

questions.stem: A farmer increases the number of cattle in their herd and also clears forest to create more grazing land. Which two greenhouse gases will increase as a result of these activities?

options.text: Oxygen and nitrogen
Carbon dioxide (from deforestation) and methane (from cattle)
Ozone and sulfur dioxide
Carbon monoxide and hydrogen

questions.explanation: Cattle produce methane (CH₄) during digestion (enteric fermentation), and their manure also releases methane. Deforestation removes trees that absorb CO₂ through photosynthesis, and if the wood is burned or decays, the stored carbon is released as CO₂. Both methane and carbon dioxide are greenhouse gases that contribute to climate change.

questions.stem: Methane (CH₄) makes up a much smaller proportion of the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, yet it is considered a significant greenhouse gas. Why?

options.text: Methane is actually more abundant than CO₂
Methane absorbs much more infrared radiation per molecule than CO₂, making it a more potent greenhouse gas
Methane destroys the ozone layer
Methane reacts with oxygen to produce more CO₂

questions.explanation: Although methane is present at much lower concentrations than CO₂, each methane molecule is approximately 80 times more effective at absorbing infrared radiation over a 20-year period. This means even small increases in methane concentration can have a significant impact on global warming. Sources include rice paddies, landfill sites, cattle, and natural gas leaks.

questions.stem: Scientists predict that climate change will cause sea levels to rise. Which two processes contribute to sea level rise?

options.text: More rain falling into the oceans and rivers flowing faster
Thermal expansion of ocean water as it warms, and melting of land-based ice sheets and glaciers
Melting of sea ice and increased evaporation
Underwater volcanic eruptions and earthquakes

questions.explanation: Sea levels rise due to two main factors: (1) thermal expansion — as ocean water warms, it expands and takes up more volume; (2) melting of land-based ice — glaciers and ice sheets on land (Greenland, Antarctica) add new water to the oceans when they melt. Note: melting of floating sea ice does not significantly change sea levels, as it already displaces its weight in water.

questions.stem: A student argues that since water vapour is actually the most abundant greenhouse gas, human CO₂ emissions do not matter. What is the flaw in this argument?

options.text: Water vapour is not a greenhouse gas
Water vapour levels are controlled by temperature through evaporation and precipitation; CO₂ increases from fossil fuels persist and drive additional warming that increases water vapour further
The student is correct — CO₂ is not important
Humans produce more water vapour than CO₂

questions.explanation: While water vapour is indeed the most abundant greenhouse gas, its concentration is controlled by temperature (warm air holds more water vapour, which condenses as rain). CO₂ from fossil fuels accumulates in the atmosphere and causes initial warming. This warming increases evaporation and water vapour, which causes further warming — a positive feedback loop. CO₂ is the driver that humans can control.
